title: SBA Loan Eligibility Requirements (2026) | SBARates.com
description: Who qualifies for an SBA loan: size standards, ineligible businesses, credit, equity injection and cash flow, with a five-minute eligibility checklist.
h1: SBA loan eligibility: who qualifies in 2026
lede: The SBA's basic eligibility rules, the businesses it won't finance, and what lenders add on top.
body:
To get an SBA loan, a business generally has to be a for-profit company operating in the U.S., meet the SBA's size standard for its industry, show it can repay from cash flow, and have owners who invest their own money and have reasonable credit. Some business types are ineligible no matter how strong they are.

The core SBA eligibility requirements

RequirementWhat it means in practice
For-profit businessNonprofits can't get 7(a) or 504 loans. (Some nonprofit child-care centers are a narrow exception for microloans.)
Operates in the U.S.The business is located in and operates mainly in the United States or its territories.
Small by SBA standardsUnder the size standard for your NAICS code, measured by revenue or employees, including affiliates. An alternative test (tangible net worth under $20 million and net income under $6.5 million) also works for 7(a) and 504.
Ability to repayCash flow covers the new payment with room to spare. Most lenders want a debt service coverage ratio of at least 1.15 to 1.25.
Owner equityOwners have money in the business. Start-ups and business purchases generally need at least 10% equity injection.
Owner character and creditOwners of 20% or more give a personal guarantee. Lenders review credit history, and owners can't be delinquent on federal debt.
Sound business purposeThe money goes to an eligible use: working capital, equipment, real estate, a business purchase or refinancing.

Businesses that can't get an SBA loan

The SBA bars certain business types regardless of size or credit. The most common ones borrowers run into:

  • Passive businesses that only hold real estate or investments to collect rent or returns, such as landlords leasing to unrelated tenants. (An eligible operating company that occupies its own building is fine.)
  • Lending and investment businesses: lenders, pawn shops that mainly lend, investment funds.
  • Speculative businesses such as oil wildcatting or buying property to flip.
  • Gambling businesses that get more than a third of revenue from gambling.
  • Businesses that are illegal under federal law, which includes cannabis businesses even where state law allows them.
  • Pyramid sales plans, private clubs that restrict membership for reasons other than capacity, and businesses primarily engaged in political or lobbying activities.
  • Government-owned entities and most businesses owned by people on parole or incarcerated (rules here were relaxed in recent years, so ask).

Eligibility vs. approval

Eligible doesn't mean approved. The SBA sets the floor, and the lender decides. A lender will look at the "five Cs": character, capacity (cash flow), capital (your equity), collateral and conditions (your industry and the economy). The SBA doesn't require full collateral, and a loan of $50,000 or less needs none, but a lender will take what is available on larger loans.

Start-ups and business buyers

Start-ups are eligible for 7(a), 504 and microloans. Expect to show direct industry or management experience, a business plan with monthly projections for the first year, and at least 10% equity. Buying an existing business is one of the most common uses of a 7(a) loan; the seller can carry part of the equity on a standby note in some cases.

Check your eligibility in five minutes

  1. Find your NAICS code and check the SBA size standard for it.
  2. Confirm your business type isn't on the ineligible list above.
  3. Add up your current debt payments and the new loan payment (use our SBA loan calculator) and compare to your cash flow.
  4. Pull your credit and resolve any federal debt delinquencies or recent tax liens.
  5. Gather your documents: see our SBA loan documentation checklist.

Then compare lenders: rates are capped, but approval appetite varies widely. See today's SBA loan rates, the SBA lenders list by state, and guides for your industry.

faqs.q: What credit score do I need for an SBA loan?
faqs.a: The SBA doesn't set a minimum personal credit score. Most banks want to see scores in the high 600s or above, and many 7(a) loans under $350,000 are also screened with a FICO SBSS business score. Mission lenders and microlenders work with lower scores.

faqs.q: Can a new business get an SBA loan?
faqs.a: Yes. Start-ups are eligible for 7(a), 504 and microloans, but lenders want relevant experience, a solid plan with projections, and at least 10% equity. A microloan or SBA Express loan is often the realistic first step.

faqs.q: Are nonprofits eligible for SBA loans?
faqs.a: Not for 7(a) or 504 loans, which require a for-profit business. Nonprofit child-care centers can use SBA microloans, and nonprofits can apply for SBA disaster loans.

faqs.q: Can I get an SBA loan with a past bankruptcy?
faqs.a: Often, yes. A bankruptcy isn't an automatic bar, but lenders will want it discharged, an explanation, and clean credit since. Several years of distance helps a lot.

faqs.q: Do I need collateral to qualify?
faqs.a: No. The SBA won't decline a loan only for lack of collateral, and loans of $50,000 or less don't require any. On larger loans the lender must take available collateral, which can include business assets and a lien on your home.

title: SBA Loan Documents Checklist (2026) | SBARates.com
description: Every document you need for an SBA loan: SBA Forms 1919 and 413, tax returns, financials, debt schedule, and extras for buying a business or real estate.
lede: The SBA forms, financial statements and legal documents lenders ask for, organized by loan purpose.
body:
Most SBA loan delays come from missing paperwork, not credit. Have the items below ready before you call a lender and you can cut weeks off approval. Requirements vary by lender and loan size; SBA Express and small 7(a) loans need less.

SBA forms

FormWho fills it outWhat it covers
SBA Form 1919 (Borrower Information Form)The business and each owner of 20% or moreOwnership, the loan request, eligibility questions, criminal history and federal debt
SBA Form 413 (Personal Financial Statement)Each owner of 20% or more, and spouses in some casesPersonal assets, liabilities, income and contingent debts
SBA Form 912 (if asked)Owners with certain criminal historyStatement of personal history; many lenders no longer require it
IRS Form 4506-CThe business and ownersLets the lender verify your tax returns with the IRS
SBA Form 1244 (504 loans)The business, through the CDCThe 504 application

Financial documents

  • Business federal tax returns for the last three years (two is enough for some lenders).
  • Personal federal tax returns for each 20%+ owner for the last three years.
  • Year-to-date profit and loss statement and balance sheet, dated within 90 days.
  • Business debt schedule: every loan, lease and line of credit with lender, balance, payment, rate and maturity.
  • Accounts receivable and payable agings, for businesses that sell on credit.
  • Recent business bank statements (lenders often ask for 3 to 12 months).

Business and legal documents

  • Articles of incorporation or organization, operating agreement or bylaws, and certificate of good standing.
  • Business licenses and permits, including industry licenses (liquor, medical, contractor, CDL).
  • Your lease, or a letter of intent from the landlord. The lease should run at least as long as the loan term, including options.
  • Franchise agreement and FDD, if you're a franchise. The brand should be on the SBA Franchise Directory.
  • Resumes for each owner and key manager, showing relevant experience.

Extra documents by loan purpose

If you are...Also prepare
Buying a businessPurchase agreement or LOI, the seller's last three years of tax returns and interim financials, list of assets included, and any seller note terms
Starting a businessBusiness plan with monthly projections for year one and annual for years two and three, source of your equity injection, and market research
Buying or building real estatePurchase contract, construction budget and contractor bids, and the property address for appraisal and environmental review
Buying equipmentVendor quotes or invoices with model numbers
Refinancing debtOriginal note and statements for the debt being refinanced, showing payment history

Tips that speed up approval

  1. Write a one-page loan request: how much, what for, how you'll repay, and what collateral you have.
  2. Explain anything unusual up front: a down year, a credit issue, a gap in tax filings.
  3. Document your equity injection: bank statements showing the cash has been in your account (lenders often ask for two months of history), or gift letters.
  4. Send everything as clearly named PDFs in one batch.

Ready to compare? See current SBA loan rates, check whether your business is eligible, and estimate payments with the SBA loan calculator.

faqs.q: How many years of tax returns do I need for an SBA loan?
faqs.a: Most lenders ask for three years of business and personal federal returns. Some accept two for smaller loans, and start-ups provide personal returns plus projections instead.
The Borrower Information Form. The business and every owner of 20% or more complete it. It covers ownership, the loan request and eligibility questions such as federal debt and criminal history.
The Personal Financial Statement. Each owner of 20% or more lists personal assets, liabilities and income so the lender can assess personal guarantees and liquidity.

faqs.q: How long does SBA loan approval take?
faqs.a: With a complete file, SBA Express loans can be approved in days and standard 7(a) loans from Preferred Lenders in a few weeks. Real estate and 504 loans often take 45 to 90 days to close because of appraisals and environmental reviews.
